deck.title: Copilot,
deck.tagline: An engineer's field guide to coding with AI — the mindset, the loop, and the Four D's of fluency.
deck.introSubtitle: How to use AI coding tools well from day one — and own every line you ship

overview.title: AI Fluency for Engineers
overview.subtitle: Having the tool is not the same as using it well — fluency is what separates the teams that gain from the teams that stall
overview.summary: Nearly half of new code is now written with AI, and developers move measurably faster. But the tool is identical for everyone — the difference is fluency. This guide gives you the one rule, the working loop, and the four skills that make AI an accelerator instead of a liability.

cards.title: Delegation
cards.body: Decide what to hand off and what to keep. Boilerplate and tests go to AI; novel, critical, and security logic stay with you.

cards.title: Description
cards.body: Say what you want precisely — context, constraints, examples, and output format. Garbage in, garbage out.

cards.title: Discernment
cards.body: Evaluate every output for correctness, security, and fit. The AI sounds confident even when it is wrong.

cards.title: Diligence
cards.body: Own it end to end: review, test, attribute, and protect data before anything merges.

talkingPoints: Open with the shift: ~46% of code in Copilot users' repos is now AI-authored, up from ~27% in 2022.
Reframe the goal: this is not 'can I use it' — it's 'can I use it well.'
Preview the Four D's as the spine of the rest of the deck.
Set the tone with the one rule: you own every line that ships.
overview.callout: The tool is the same for everyone. Fluency is the difference.

human.title: Human in the Loop
human.heroTitle: The One Rule: You Own Every Line
human.subkicker: Treat AI as a junior pair programmer
human.subtitle: AI accelerates the work. Human judgment governs the quality.
human.thesis: Accelerated by AI. Owned by the engineer.

cards.title: Plan Before You Code
cards.highlight: Clarify requirements and sketch the approach before you prompt.
details: Write acceptance criteria and consider edge cases first.
Pseudo-code the outline in comments, then let AI fill the blanks.
A vague prompt like 'make my app faster' produces the wrong optimization.

cards.title: Prompt With Context
cards.highlight: Context, constraints, examples, and output format turn guesses into usable code.
details: Tell it your standards: 'use our internal logger, not console.log.'
One team cut reformatting of AI output by 80% by embedding style rules in prompts.
Work incrementally — one function or module at a time, not one giant request.

cards.title: Review & Verify
cards.highlight: Every AI-assisted line is reviewed and tested as if a human junior wrote it.
details: No AI-authored code merges until a human and/or static analysis vets it.
Snyk, Checkmarx, and CodeQL catch many AI-introduced bugs.
A second AI pass can audit or write tests — but a human still approves.

leadershipPoints: Automation bias is the real risk: a Stanford study found AI-assisted developers wrote more insecure code and were more confident it was safe.
Humans keep release authority even when AI authors most of the implementation.
Review rigor is what makes the speed credible.

results.label: Faster task completion
results.detail: in a controlled GitHub/Accenture trial with thousands of developers

results.label: Shorter PR cycle time
results.detail: mean time to merge fell from 9.6 days to 2.4 days

results.label: Of code now AI-authored
results.detail: in Copilot users' repositories by mid-2025 (61% for Java)

results.label: Of accepted suggestions kept
results.detail: remain unchanged in the final code once a developer accepts them

human.enablement: An Anthropic study found developers who asked the AI follow-up questions improved over time, while those who passively accepted answers did worse on comprehension. Use AI as a teacher, not a crutch.
human.callout: AI generates code. Humans own the decisions.

hurdles.title: Failure Modes & Fixes
hurdles.subtitle: The four ways AI coding goes wrong — and the discipline that prevents each

cards.title: Hallucinated Packages
cards.challenge: AI invents plausible-but-fake imports; attackers publish real malicious packages under those names ('slopsquatting').
cards.fix: Verify every suggested dependency against official sources; use package allow-lists.

cards.title: Insecure by Default
cards.challenge: Roughly 30% of AI-generated snippets carried a vulnerability — SQLi, XSS, hard-coded credentials, weak crypto.
cards.fix: Security-review every AI line and gate merges with static analysis (Snyk, CodeQL).

cards.title: Vague Prompts
cards.challenge: Under-specified, one-shot prompts produce confident solutions to the wrong problem.
cards.fix: Provide context, constraints, and examples; break work into small, reviewable steps.

cards.title: Skill Atrophy
cards.challenge: Passively accepting output erodes understanding — and inflates false confidence.
cards.fix: Ask the AI to explain; treat it as a pair partner you mentor and question.

hurdles.callout: Every failure mode has a known fix — and the fix is engineering discipline, not a better model.

sprint.title: The Working Loop
sprint.subtitle: Plan → Generate → Review, in small cycles — with human checkpoints at every stage
sprint.callout: The loop keeps the AI on a short leash: plan the intent, generate a small piece, review it, repeat.

future.title: Where AI Shines
future.subtitle: Point AI at the work it does best — and know where the field is heading

cards.title: Boilerplate & Tests
cards.body: CRUD, data models, and unit-test scaffolds come 2–3× faster — the AI rarely gets these wrong.

cards.title: Translate & Refactor
cards.body: Port code between languages and modernize idioms in a strong first draft you then review.

cards.title: Docs & Navigation
cards.body: Generate docstrings and READMEs, and explain unfamiliar code or large codebases on demand.

cards.title: What's Next
cards.body: Agentic coding and whole-codebase reasoning are arriving — with human approval checkpoints built in.

future.callout: Aim AI at boilerplate, tests, translation, and explanation — and keep judgment where it belongs.

platform.title: Boundaries & The Hard Rules
platform.subtitle: When not to reach for AI — and the non-negotiables that keep client and code safe
platform.summary: Fluency includes knowing the limits. Some work belongs to humans, and some data never goes into any AI tool. These boundaries are what let the team move fast everywhere else.

focusPanels.label: When Not To
focusPanels.title: Human-only work
focusPanels.body: Novel algorithms, security-critical code, and regulated/traceable software stay with experienced engineers.

focusPanels.label: Hard Rules
focusPanels.title: Data you never paste
focusPanels.body: No CUI, PII, or credentials in any AI tool — ever. Use sanitized examples and approved tools only.

focusPanels.label: Across the SDLC
focusPanels.title: Use it everywhere it's safe
focusPanels.body: Design, tests-first TDD, refactoring, docs, and learning all benefit — under the same review discipline.

capabilities.title: Critical Algorithms
capabilities.body: Novel or complex business logic — design it yourself first.

capabilities.title: Security Code
capabilities.body: Auth, encryption, and input validation — assist only, never autopilot.

capabilities.title: Regulated Code
capabilities.body: Aerospace, medical, and audited systems need traceability AI can't yet provide.

capabilities.title: Poor-Data Domains
capabilities.body: Proprietary or obscure stacks where the model is out of its depth.

lanes.title: Green-Light Zone
lanes.subtitle: AI accelerates · standard review
lanes.persona: User: Any engineer, with normal code review and tests
steps: Draft boilerplate, CRUD, and data models.
Generate unit-test scaffolds and edge cases.
Refactor, translate, and document existing code.

lanes.title: Human-Only Zone
lanes.subtitle: Senior / security review required
lanes.persona: User: Experienced engineer; AI assists at most
steps: Design novel algorithms and core business logic.
Write and review security- and safety-critical code.
Handle regulated or audited systems requiring traceability.

talkingPoints: Frame boundaries as enabling speed, not limiting it — clear rules remove hesitation.
The hard data rules are absolute: no CUI, PII, or credentials in any AI tool.
Get client sign-off before using AI on client code.
Everywhere outside the human-only zone, lean in — under the same review discipline.
platform.callout: Know the limits, protect the data, and the team can move fast everywhere else.
